plan.contextChunk: This figure contains two 2D vectors emanating from a common origin, illustrating the geometric definition of endpoint error in optical flow evaluation. The vector labeled (u, v) represents the ground truth flow vector, while the vector labeled (u-hat, v-hat) represents the predicted flow vector; both share the same base point but point in slightly different directions and have different magnitudes. A red line segment connects the tips (endpoints) of the two vectors, and this segment is labeled Endpoint error, making explicit that the loss is the Euclidean distance between the endpoint of the prediction and the endpoint of the ground truth. This figure establishes endpoint error as a vector-space distance metric, clarifying why it is sensitive to both directional and magnitude errors in the predicted flow field.

interactionPlan.concept: Endpoint error combines both magnitude and directional discrepancies into a single Euclidean distance between vector tips.
elements: Ground truth vector (u, v) drawn as a black arrow pointing up and right
Predicted vector (u-hat, v-hat) drawn as a black arrow pointing right and slightly up
Label '(u, v)' near the tip of the ground truth vector
Label '(u-hat, v-hat)' near the tip of the predicted vector
Red line segment connecting the two vector tips
Label 'Endpoint error' next to the red line segment
Red arc between the two vectors near the origin
Label 'Angular error' next to the red arc

interactions.label: Predicted u
interactions.teaches: Changing the horizontal component of the predicted flow vector shifts its tip, directly altering the length of the error segment.

interactions.label: Predicted v
interactions.teaches: Changing the vertical component of the predicted flow vector changes both its magnitude and angle relative to the ground truth.

interactions.label: Error metric
interactions.teaches: Endpoint error captures the straight-line Euclidean distance between tips, while angular error isolates the directional difference.

demo_steps.title: Endpoint error
demo_steps.narration: Endpoint error is the Euclidean distance between the predicted and true flow vectors, effectively combining both magnitude and direction penalties into a single metric.

demo_steps.title: Angular error
demo_steps.narration: Toggling to angular error isolates the directional mismatch. It measures only the angle between the vectors, ignoring differences in their lengths.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Endpoint error is a comprehensive metric because it geometrically measures the exact distance between where a pixel actually moved and where it was predicted to move.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Do not draw coordinate axes; just the vectors floating in space emanating from a shared origin at the bottom left. The ground truth vector (u,v) should be fixed, pointing steeply up and right. The predicted vector updates based on the sliders. In 'Endpoint error' mode, display only the red line segment between the vector tips and its label. In 'Angular error' mode, display only the red arc connecting the two vectors near the origin and its label. Use math styling for (u, v) and (u-hat, v-hat).

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Drag the estimated vector tip (û,v̂) in any direction and see the red endpoint error segment stretch or shrink in real time as the distance between the two vector tips updates
- Drag the ground-truth vector tip (u,v) to set a new reference flow direction and magnitude, watching the red error segment reposition accordingly
- Toggle between endpoint error (straight-line distance between vector tips) and angular error (angle between the two vectors) metrics, highlighting which geometric quantity each measures in the diagram

authoredContext: In supervised optical flow estimation, the most common loss is the **endpoint error**, which is the average, over the whole image, if the distance between the estimated optical flow vector, $(\hat{u},\hat{v})$ and the ground-truth vector, $(u,v)$: $$\mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \right) = \sum_{n,m} (\hat{u}[n,m] - u[n,m])^2 + (\hat{v}[n,m] - v[n,m])^2$$ The sum is over all the pixels in the image. Each pixel has an estimated optical flow $(\hat{u}[n,m],\hat{v}[n,m])$.
